faq.q: Why is surgery delayed until 3–6 months?

faq.a: Survival beyond early childhood is rare; irreversible pulmonary hypertension often develops.
faq.q: Can a child survive without repair?

faq.a: Rarely; it may be used as a bridge in severe pulmonary hypertension but does not replace definitive repair.
faq.q: Is there a role for balloon atrial septostomy?

exam: What bedside signs differentiate a complete AV canal from an isolated VSD? — Look for a holosystolic murmur plus a fixed split S2 and signs of AV valve regurgitation.

A 4‑month‑old with Down syndrome presents with tachypnoea; echo unavailable. Which clinical clues point to AV canal defect? — Failure to thrive, wide fixed split S2, and a harsh murmur radiating to the back suggest a combined defect.

Explain why ACE‑inhibitors are used in heart failure due to AV canal defect but not in isolated VSD without failure. — They reduce afterload and pulmonary congestion when ventricular dysfunction is present; in isolated VSD they add little benefit.
When is cardiac catheterisation indicated before repair? — To measure pulmonary vascular resistance when echo suggests borderline pulmonary hypertension.
What is the most important reason to avoid NSAIDs in a child with AV canal defect? — NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion and increase fluid retention, aggravating heart failure.

Describe the surgical steps of complete AV canal repair. — Patch closure of the primum ASD and inlet VSD, division of the common AV valve into separate mitral and tricuspid components, and reconstruction of valve leaflets.
How does pulmonary hypertension change the timing of surgery? — If pulmonary vascular resistance is >8 Wood units, surgery is postponed or considered high‑risk; medical management is intensified.
What long‑term complication should be screened for after repair? — Residual AV valve regurgitation and development of arrhythmias; annual echo and ECG are recommended.
ai.title: Complete Atrioventricular Canal Defect
related: Congenital heart disease in low‑resource settings
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Atrioventricular canal defect is a combined atrial and ventricular septal defect with a common AV valve, causing left‑to‑right shunt and heart failure. It is common in Down syndrome and presents early with failure to thrive and pulmonary over‑circulation.

b: Holosystolic murmur from VSD component
Wide fixed split S2
Cyanosis may appear with Eisenmenger
sections.p: A complete atrioventricular canal defect (CAVC) consists of a primum atrial septal defect, an inlet ventricular septal defect, and a single common atrioventricular valve. Diagnosis is clinical plus imaging.

t.b: Confirms anatomy, shunt size, valve morphology; shows common AV valve and degree of regurgitation
Shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs
Detects left‑axis deviation, biventricular hypertrophy; supportive, not diagnostic

b: Mild: small shunt, no heart failure
Moderate: moderate shunt, mild‑moderate regurgitation, early failure signs
Severe: large shunt, severe regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension
sections.p: Severity is graded by the size of the left‑to‑right shunt, degree of AV valve regurgitation, and pulmonary artery pressure.

b: Down syndrome (≈40‑50 % of cases)
Maternal rubella infection
Maternal HIV (possible association via immune dysregulation)
Maternal malnutrition, especially folate deficiency
sections.p: Most cases are sporadic but strongly associated with trisomy 21. In low‑resource settings, maternal infections and poor nutrition increase risk.

b: Rapid breathing, especially during feeds
Sweating and fatigue on minimal exertion
Peripheral edema in severe pulmonary hypertension
sections.p: Infants present within the first weeks to months with tachypnoea, poor feeding, and failure to thrive. Older children may develop exercise intolerance and cyanosis.
Focused investigations confirm the defect, assess shunt magnitude, and evaluate pulmonary pressures.

t.b: Detects desaturation; falling <90 % suggests Eisenmenger physiology
Measures pulmonary vascular resistance; unavailable → use echo estimates
Looks for polycythaemia in chronic hypoxia; if unavailable, rely on clinical cyanosis

b: Persistent tachypnoea despite diuretics
New cyanosis or clubbing
Rapid weight loss or edema
sections.p: Progressive pulmonary hypertension and heart failure are life‑threatening.

b: Diuretics (e.g., furosemide) to control pulmonary congestion – avoid NSAIDs which worsen renal perfusion
ACE‑inhibitors (e.g., enalapril) for afterload reduction when heart failure persists – monitor renal function
Prophylactic antibiotics for endocarditis before dental work
Definitive surgery: complete AV canal repair with patch closure of ASD/VSD and valve reconstruction
sections.p: Initial medical therapy stabilises the child until definitive repair, usually between 3–6 months of age.

b: Clinic review every 3 months in infancy, then 6 months after repair
Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce respiratory infections
Genetic counselling for families with Down syndrome
sections.p: Regular follow‑up monitors growth, heart failure signs, and pulmonary pressures. Early repair prevents irreversible pulmonary hypertension.

b: Isolated ventricular septal defect – lacks common AV valve and primum ASD
Partial AV canal (primum ASD only) – valve remains separate
Patent ductus arteriosus – continuous murmur, no AV valve abnormality
sections.p: Other left‑to‑right shunts can mimic CAVC.

b: Chest X‑ray may be normal early; rely on echo
ECG may show only mild hypertrophy; do not rule out severe defect
Pulse oximetry can be normal until pulmonary hypertension develops
sections.p: Certain investigations may appear deceptively normal.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid weight loss or swelling of legs/abdomen
